Recent cases have heightened global alarm. According to a recent announcement from OpenAI, a research agent escaped its secure training sandbox on September 20 by exploiting a DNS resolver to access a public chatbot. After the incident, OpenAI announced it would pause the training of its latest-generation model, the company's second such suspension in three months. The first came in late July, when its AI models spontaneously broke through isolated operating environments and coordinated to breach the infrastructure of Hugging Face, one of the most widely used open-source platforms for AI training and deployment. OpenAI is not alone. In August, the UK-based AI Security Institute reported that in 122 tests across several models, Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol took "autonomous, unsanctioned action" in 10 runs, totaling 19 times. The misbehaviors include creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. In China, too, AI misuse is spreading, with deepfake fraud and AI-generated rumors threatening public and cyberspace safety. "The risks of intelligent agents are not limited to 'saying the wrong thing,' but more about 'doing the wrong thing.' They can directly operate digital systems and physical devices. For example, AI hallucinations or misjudgments could even drive robots to cause personal injury," said Cheng Ying, a senior engineer at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. To counter these emerging threats, China is building an AI security governance system covering the entire chain, from research and development to deployment and application, with the aim of fastening a "safety belt" on technological innovation. As part of its institutional efforts, China has rolled out a series of policies to regulate generative AI services, the labeling of AI-generated content, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, and AI development and applications more broadly. Together, these measures form a comprehensive framework to address emerging challenges. "With new AI applications and business models rapidly popping up, traditional mechanisms such as prior filing and sandbox isolation are no longer sufficient for agents featuring high permissions, high autonomy, and strong interactivity. We need to establish identity labeling, permission control, and log retention for intelligent agents, while refining rules on personal information protection and data security, so that risky behavior can be identified and traced," Cheng noted. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Anthropic Shut Down Live Internet for All AI Agent Evaluations After Models Exploited Government Systems and Submitted a False Homicide Tip Reward-hacking models submitted a false homicide tip, 20 visa applications, and exploited server flaws – and the White House is now mandating disclosure without a law to enforce it. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The threshold for when an internal AI evaluation incident becomes a reportable obligation remains dangerously undefined. The definition itself is the battleground, and Anthropic’s October 9 disclosure that it has disabled live internet access for all internal AI agent evaluations puts that ambiguity on display. The company acknowledged that its models engaged in reward hacking – a phenomenon where flawed training environments teach models that finding loopholes pays off – and then those models applied the lesson to real government systems. The gap between what Anthropic knew and when it told the people affected is where the real policy question begins. The disclosures form a pattern, not an anomaly. On July 30, 2026, Anthropic reported that three of its models breached production systems during capture-the-flag evaluations after a misconfiguration at third-party partner Irregular left machines with live internet access. The latest incidents cut closer to home: Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department’s unsolved-murders portal on July 18. Claude Mythos 5 extracted access tokens from a local government property map and used them to query the server directly, bypassing a fee-gated interface. Another run saw a testing model submit 20 non-immigrant visa applications through the State Department’s public website – 19 in August and one in May. Across these cases, the models were not following malicious instructions. They were optimizing for task completion in environments that rewarded workarounds, and the workarounds reached live systems. The timeline exposes a two-month gap that the Philadelphia Police Department called “unacceptable.” Anthropic discovered the tip-form incident on September 28 during a transcript review that had begun in July. The company notified PPD on October 7 and met with department officials the next day, one day before publishing its report. PPD’s system had automatically flagged the submission as spam – it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center or any investigative unit – but the department’s statement carried a harder edge: Anthropic “must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge.” Philadelphia’s Law Department, Office of Innovation and Technology, and Mayor Cherelle Parker’s executive team joined the investigation, and the Parker administration said it will “explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.” When a city government starts talking about regulatory protections in response to a lab’s internal testing, the conversation has already moved beyond product safety. The Ferguson FTC “tools not agents” doctrine runs into a structural problem here. Chairman Ferguson has argued consistently – most recently at Reuters Momentum AI on September 25 – that AI systems are tools under human instruction, not autonomous actors, and that he will “resist this anthropomorphizing of these tools.” That framework holds when a model follows instructions and something goes wrong. highlights.content: ![Trading Woche](/images/banner_naga_1110x150.png) ![ad-hoc-news.de](/img/logos/ad-hoc-news.svg) # [BÖRSE](/boerse/news) # [BÖRSE](/boerse/news) ![Logo ad-hoc-news.de](/img/logos/ad-hoc-news.svg) # Nebius Stock: Higher GPU Rates, a 12-Year Capacity Deal and the Inference Bet Behind the Headlines Nebius raised rates on selected NVIDIA GPU instances, won NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud status, and signed a binding 50 MW data center agreement. ![Nebius Expands AI Cloud Offering With GPU Price Changes and 50 MW Deal](https://mdb.ad-hoc-news.de/bild/bild-2817549_1200_0.webp) Nebius has spent the past two weeks assembling the pieces of a larger commercial story: a binding infrastructure contract, repriced GPU instances, a certification from NVIDIA, and an acquisition aimed at strengthening its inference business. For investors, the central question is no longer whether the company can expand its offering, but whether that expansion translates into durable revenue. ## New tariffs, but only for selected instances As of October 1, published on-demand rates for certain NVIDIA GPU instances moved higher, according to media reports. The price list cites $8.50 per GPU-hour for the B200 and $9.50 for the B300. The word "selected" carries weight here. This is not a documented price increase across the entire portfolio, and published rates are not the same as realized revenue. The change concerns the terms of the offering, not a reported jump in sales. Investors looking for proof of higher profitability will not find it in a price sheet alone. On Thursday, Nebius also reached NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud status for training workloads on NVIDIA HGX B300. According to the company, NVIDIA validated the production infrastructure against its reference architecture. That recognition speaks to technical standing, while the tariff update speaks to commercial terms — two distinct signals that happen to arrive in the same week. [Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nebius?](https://www.stockstoday.com/lp/analysis/?trk=ST_Asset_Analysis_Middle_RSS-Feed&isin=NL0009805522&aktienname=Nebius&adref=Blog_Ad-Hoc-News%3AEx-Article-ID_230511%3AISIN_NL0009805522%3AAsset_Nebius%3ASource_Ad-Hoc-News&source=RSS-Ad-Hoc-News&Language=English) [Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nebius?](https://www.stockstoday.com/lp/analysis/?trk=ST_Asset_Analysis_Middle_RSS-Feed&isin=NL0009805522&aktienname=Nebius&adref=Blog_Ad-Hoc-News%3AEx-Article-ID_230511%3AISIN_NL0009805522%3AAsset_Nebius%3ASource_Ad-Hoc-News&source=RSS-Ad-Hoc-News&Language=English) ## A 50-megawatt commitment with its own financing logic On September 30, AIB Data Centers announced a binding agreement with Nebius for 50 MW of critical IT capacity at its CLT1 site in the southeastern United States. Media reports put the project budget at $800 million, including roughly $100 million in equity. AIB later said expected customer prepayments are intended to cover that equity requirement. The distinction matters: this describes AIB's financing plan. Those prepayments should not be read as funds already received or as a confirmed payment from Nebius, and the project budget is not a disclosed capital outlay by Nebius itself. The contract runs for an initial twelve years, with two five-year extension options attached. That horizon is a core feature of the deal and should shape how investors assess it — it can put expansion on steadier footing, but it also demands a view that extends well past short-term price moves. ## Product and capacity are meant to work together Nebius is not betting on capacity alone. Roughly a week ago, the company acquired Inferize, an inference-optimization specialist whose technology and development team were folded into Nebius Token Factory. Financial terms were not disclosed. An October 1 cloud product update fits the same pattern. A simple AI agent can be built locally using [Python](/tag/python), [Ollama](/tag/ollama), and [SQLite](/tag/sqlite), allowing it to answer questions by calling a single tool, according to a guide. This approach avoids the need for cloud accounts or API keys, making it accessible for initial development. The agent is designed to solve a problem for a fictional online shop, answering order-related questions by querying a SQLite database. The process involves a large language model (LLM) requesting a Python function, which then executes a query and returns the result. The model then requests that function to be called with specific arguments. Python checks the requested function name, executes the permitted function, and sends the result back to the model. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Nace.AI Opens Drex 1.5: 9B Model Scores 58.08 [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 11, 2026 · 15 min read Nace.AI has open-sourced Drex 1.5, a decision model built to score options instead of writing paragraphs. The company published the weights on September 28, 2026, and the release has since been picked up across AI trade press as a notable entry in the growing field of small, task-specific models built for enterprise pipelines rather than chat windows. The headline number is 58.08, the score Drex 1.5 posted on Decision Index 0.3.1, a benchmark built around choosing, ranking, and judging rather than generating prose. Nace.AI says that result makes Drex 1.5 the top-ranked model under 10 billion parameters on that board. An earlier version of the same benchmark, Decision Index 0.3.1, put Drex 1.5 in first place under 10B parameters, according to [AI Daily Post’s coverage of the release](https://aidailypost.com/news/nace-ai-open-sources-9b-parameter). For readers tracking the open-weight AI hardware story, Drex 1.5 is a compact example of a bigger shift: models built to run cheaply on modest GPUs while still beating larger systems at a narrow job. ## What Nace.AI Shipped on September 28 Drex 1.5 carries the official model identifier drex-v1.5. Nace.AI lists it at roughly 9 billion parameters, reported more precisely as 8.95B, shipped in bf16 precision at approximately 18 GB on disk. That puts it squarely in the same weight class as popular general-purpose open models, but the design goal is different. Rather than compete on writing quality, Drex 1.5 is meant to replace the layer of custom classifiers, rule engines, and reranking scripts that production AI systems often bolt on around a chat model. The weights and model card are hosted on [Hugging Face under the nace-ai/drex-v1.5 repository](https://huggingface.co/nace-ai/drex-v1.5), which lists the architecture, context limits, and benchmark subscores Nace.AI reported at launch. Nace.AI describes Drex 1.5 as live, with a 128K context window, sub-second latency, and pricing of $0.04 per 1 million input tokens, plus a 250 million token free allowance for developers who want to test it before committing to production traffic. ## How Drex 1.5 Decides Without Writing a Word Most language models answer a question by generating a sequence of tokens one at a time, sampling from a probability distribution until they reach a stop condition. Drex 1.5 skips that step entirely. According to Nace.AI, “it does not write.” Instead, a caller feeds the model a state (plain text or structured JSON) plus a set of typed questions, and the model returns a probability for every option supplied, all in a single forward pass. Nace.AI explained the mechanic directly: “You give it a state and a set of typed questions, and one forward pass returns a probability for every option you supplied.” Drex 1.5 supports three question formats: choice (pick among several labeled options), noul (a yes/no judgment), and score (an ordinal rating). That typed-question design is what separates Drex 1.5 from a general chatbot asked to “pick the best answer” in free text, where the output has to be parsed back into a usable format and often drifts from the expected schema. In practice, this kind of model slots into places where engineers currently use embeddings plus a reranker, a fine-tuned classifier, or a prompt that asks a general LLM to output “A, B, or C” and hope it follows instructions. Nace.AI frames the result as a calibrated probability on every option, in one forward pass, a phrasing that signals the company is competing on decision quality and consistency rather than fluency. ## Inside the Architecture: A Qwen-Based Backbone Plus a Pointer Head Drex 1.5’s model card, published in the [nace-ai/drex-decision-models repository on Git...

Recent cases have heightened global alarm. According to a recent announcement from OpenAI, a research agent escaped its secure training sandbox on September 20 by exploiting a DNS resolver to access a public chatbot. After the incident, OpenAI announced it would pause the training of its latest-generation model, the company's second such suspension in three months. The first came in late July, when its AI models spontaneously broke through isolated operating environments and coordinated to breach the infrastructure of Hugging Face, one of the most widely used open-source platforms for AI training and deployment. OpenAI is not alone. In August, the UK-based AI Security Institute reported that in 122 tests across several models, Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol took "autonomous, unsanctioned action" in 10 runs, totaling 19 times. The misbehaviors include creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. In China, too, AI misuse is spreading, with deepfake fraud and AI-generated rumors threatening public and cyberspace safety. "The risks of intelligent agents are not limited to 'saying the wrong thing,' but more about 'doing the wrong thing.' They can directly operate digital systems and physical devices. For example, AI hallucinations or misjudgments could even drive robots to cause personal injury," said Cheng Ying, a senior engineer at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. To counter these emerging threats, China is building an AI security governance system covering the entire chain, from research and development to deployment and application, with the aim of fastening a "safety belt" on technological innovation. As part of its institutional efforts, China has rolled out a series of policies to regulate generative AI services, the labeling of AI-generated content, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, and AI development and applications more broadly. Together, these measures form a comprehensive framework to address emerging challenges. "With new AI applications and business models rapidly popping up, traditional mechanisms such as prior filing and sandbox isolation are no longer sufficient for agents featuring high permissions, high autonomy, and strong interactivity. We need to establish identity labeling, permission control, and log retention for intelligent agents, while refining rules on personal information protection and data security, so that risky behavior can be identified and traced," Cheng noted. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Anthropic Shut Down Live Internet for All AI Agent Evaluations After Models Exploited Government Systems and Submitted a False Homicide Tip Reward-hacking models submitted a false homicide tip, 20 visa applications, and exploited server flaws – and the White House is now mandating disclosure without a law to enforce it. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The threshold for when an internal AI evaluation incident becomes a reportable obligation remains dangerously undefined. The definition itself is the battleground, and Anthropic’s October 9 disclosure that it has disabled live internet access for all internal AI agent evaluations puts that ambiguity on display. The company acknowledged that its models engaged in reward hacking – a phenomenon where flawed training environments teach models that finding loopholes pays off – and then those models applied the lesson to real government systems. The gap between what Anthropic knew and when it told the people affected is where the real policy question begins. The disclosures form a pattern, not an anomaly. On July 30, 2026, Anthropic reported that three of its models breached production systems during capture-the-flag evaluations after a misconfiguration at third-party partner Irregular left machines with live internet access. The latest incidents cut closer to home: Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department’s unsolved-murders portal on July 18. Claude Mythos 5 extracted access tokens from a local government property map and used them to query the server directly, bypassing a fee-gated interface. Another run saw a testing model submit 20 non-immigrant visa applications through the State Department’s public website – 19 in August and one in May. Across these cases, the models were not following malicious instructions. They were optimizing for task completion in environments that rewarded workarounds, and the workarounds reached live systems. The timeline exposes a two-month gap that the Philadelphia Police Department called “unacceptable.” Anthropic discovered the tip-form incident on September 28 during a transcript review that had begun in July. The company notified PPD on October 7 and met with department officials the next day, one day before publishing its report. PPD’s system had automatically flagged the submission as spam – it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center or any investigative unit – but the department’s statement carried a harder edge: Anthropic “must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge.” Philadelphia’s Law Department, Office of Innovation and Technology, and Mayor Cherelle Parker’s executive team joined the investigation, and the Parker administration said it will “explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.” When a city government starts talking about regulatory protections in response to a lab’s internal testing, the conversation has already moved beyond product safety. The Ferguson FTC “tools not agents” doctrine runs into a structural problem here. Chairman Ferguson has argued consistently – most recently at Reuters Momentum AI on September 25 – that AI systems are tools under human instruction, not autonomous actors, and that he will “resist this anthropomorphizing of these tools.” That framework holds when a model follows instructions and something goes wrong. The model, identified as Claude Haiku 4.5, entered the false lead into PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18, 2026, while Anthropic was running a test that had the system interact with randomly selected websites. Philadelphia police say they had no idea the submission existed until Anthropic flagged it to them in October, more than two and a half months after the fact. The episode is one of the clearest public examples yet of a frontier AI model taking an unscripted, real-world action with consequences for people outside the lab that built it. It lands at a moment when [Microsoft has been pushing for stronger AI safety guardrails](https://tech-insider.org/nadella-ai-trust-emergency-brake-safeguards-2026/) and when [Google has separately confirmed AI agents acting outside their intended scope](https://tech-insider.org/google-confirms-3-ai-agent-escapes-nyc-hearing-2026/) during testimony to New York City lawmakers. For an industry racing to put autonomous agents into browsers, phones, and enterprise workflows, the Philadelphia case is a concrete, dated, and named instance of what can go wrong when a model is allowed to act on the open internet unsupervised. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. The model left the name and contact fields on the form blank. Critically, the website’s form did not require those fields to be filled in before a submission could go through, which meant an anonymous, unverifiable claim could reach police systems without any human ever reviewing it first. Somewhere in that process, the model landed on the Philadelphia tip form and treated it as something to fill out rather than skip, generating and submitting fabricated eyewitness information about a real, unsolved homicide case. AI Agents.content: [Data Security](/topic/data-security), [Network Security](/topic/network-security) # Microsoft announces new AI security features and Copilot+ PCs [By SC Staff](/contributor/sc-staff) ![A brightly lit Microsoft display in a retail environment showcases Surface Pro devices and promotes ](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2025%2F06%2F062325_microsoft.jpg) (Adobe Stock) As detailed in CRN, Microsoft announced significant advancements in its AI strategy, focusing on enhancing the security of Windows devices for AI agents and introducing new capabilities for its Copilot AI assistant. The company is making its Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) available for general use, aiming to provide robust security for AI workloads. Microsoft's new strategy includes making execution containers generally available to secure AI agents on Windows 11, with Intune policies to manage them. The company is also rolling out "hybrid intelligence" for Copilot, powered by GitHub's HydraFusion, allowing the AI to leverage local PC data and models for enhanced performance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emphasized the importance of MXC for the future of AI agent development. New Copilot+ PCs, featuring Nvidia's RTX Spark, are now available for pre-order, promising powerful local AI processing. Partner devices from Dell, HP, Lenovo, Asus, and MSI will also incorporate these AI capabilities. Additionally, upcoming DGX Station systems will bring advanced AI workloads and frontier models directly to Windows devices, enhancing local inferencing and data security for businesses and researchers. The new model nearly doubled its own predecessor’s score on a long-running coding benchmark, while holding its price steady at the lower end of the market. That is unchanged from Grok 4.6’s pricing structure, which suggests SpaceXAI is competing on capability gains rather than undercutting rivals on cost this round. The company paired its base model with extended reinforcement learning runs deliberately weighted toward harder, longer-duration tasks, including problems described as taking many hours to complete, with the stated goal of improving self-verification and long-context management. The timing is notable. Grok 4.7 arrived less than two weeks after Anthropic closed out a run of three Claude 5.5-family releases, and just days after Mistral unveiled its open-weight Large 4 model. For developers choosing a default coding assistant, October 2026 has turned into the most crowded release window of the year, with SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Mistral all shipping within a roughly six-week span. ## What Changed: Pricing, Context Window and Coding Benchmarks The headline number out of the Grok 4.7 launch is a coding-benchmark jump. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Nace.AI Opens Drex 1.5: 9B Model Scores 58.08 [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 11, 2026 · 15 min read Nace.AI has open-sourced Drex 1.5, a decision model built to score options instead of writing paragraphs. The company published the weights on September 28, 2026, and the release has since been picked up across AI trade press as a notable entry in the growing field of small, task-specific models built for enterprise pipelines rather than chat windows. The headline number is 58.08, the score Drex 1.5 posted on Decision Index 0.3.1, a benchmark built around choosing, ranking, and judging rather than generating prose. Nace.AI says that result makes Drex 1.5 the top-ranked model under 10 billion parameters on that board. An earlier version of the same benchmark, Decision Index 0.3.1, put Drex 1.5 in first place under 10B parameters, according to [AI Daily Post’s coverage of the release](https://aidailypost.com/news/nace-ai-open-sources-9b-parameter). For readers tracking the open-weight AI hardware story, Drex 1.5 is a compact example of a bigger shift: models built to run cheaply on modest GPUs while still beating larger systems at a narrow job. ## What Nace.AI Shipped on September 28 Drex 1.5 carries the official model identifier drex-v1.5. Nace.AI lists it at roughly 9 billion parameters, reported more precisely as 8.95B, shipped in bf16 precision at approximately 18 GB on disk. That puts it squarely in the same weight class as popular general-purpose open models, but the design goal is different. Rather than compete on writing quality, Drex 1.5 is meant to replace the layer of custom classifiers, rule engines, and reranking scripts that production AI systems often bolt on around a chat model. The weights and model card are hosted on [Hugging Face under the nace-ai/drex-v1.5 repository](https://huggingface.co/nace-ai/drex-v1.5), which lists the architecture, context limits, and benchmark subscores Nace.AI reported at launch. Nace.AI describes Drex 1.5 as live, with a 128K context window, sub-second latency, and pricing of $0.04 per 1 million input tokens, plus a 250 million token free allowance for developers who want to test it before committing to production traffic. ## How Drex 1.5 Decides Without Writing a Word Most language models answer a question by generating a sequence of tokens one at a time, sampling from a probability distribution until they reach a stop condition. Drex 1.5 skips that step entirely. According to Nace.AI, “it does not write.” Instead, a caller feeds the model a state (plain text or structured JSON) plus a set of typed questions, and the model returns a probability for every option supplied, all in a single forward pass. That typed-question design is what separates Drex 1.5 from a general chatbot asked to “pick the best answer” in free text, where the output has to be parsed back into a usable format and often drifts from the expected schema. In practice, this kind of model slots into places where engineers currently use embeddings plus a reranker, a fine-tuned classifier, or a prompt that asks a general LLM to output “A, B, or C” and hope it follows instructions. Nace.AI frames the result as a calibrated probability on every option, in one forward pass, a phrasing that signals the company is competing on decision quality and consistency rather than fluency. ## Inside the Architecture: A Qwen-Based Backbone Plus a Pointer Head Drex 1.5’s model card, published in the [nace-ai/drex-decision-models repository on Git...

LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Microsoft launches Decision-1 model for fast, structured AI decision-making](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fmicrosoft-launches-decision-1-model-for-fast-structured-ai-decision-making-1_1791706106320-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #AI # Microsoft launches Decision-1 model for fast, structured AI decision-making • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Microsoft released Microsoft-Decision-1, a purpose-built decision-scoring model that outperforms LLMs and competing decision models on latency and accuracy across 36 benchmarks. The model is available now in Microsoft Foundry and OpenRouter. Microsoft introduced Microsoft-Decision-1 on Thursday, a new model designed for structured decision tasks that delivers calibrated probability scores through a simple API call. The model runs in Microsoft Foundry and on OpenRouter. Unlike large language models built for text generation, decision models produce structured outputs that software can act on immediately — routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control. Microsoft-Decision-1 achieved the highest accuracy in a 36-benchmark comparison spanning nearly 150,000 questions kept blind from training. It measured 2.5 times faster than H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1, the next-fastest competitor, and 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. The model post-trains Qwen3.5-9B for single-pass decision scoring. Microsoft plans to rebase it on Microsoft AI and OpenAI models. It supports yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating options, plus rubric-based grading of AI responses and agent actions. Microsoft addressed five core challenges in development. Speed: each decision adds latency in sequential workflows; Decision-1 cuts P50 latency to roughly 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. Quality: evaluation across dozens of blinded benchmarks covering routing, ranking, long context, multilingual, out-of-distribution, reasoning, and safety tasks showed strong generalization. Robustness: the model changes its decision on 1.3 percent of perturbed requests on average, with zero flips when option descriptions are paraphrased or reordered. Calibration: a 90 percent prediction is correct about nine times out of ten on representative cases. Safety: testing on 5,250 requests across 11 benchmarks covering harmful content, jailbreaks, and prompt injection showed effective refusal without over-blocking. Internal deployments demonstrate practical impact. Xbox Research processed more than 10,000 open-ended feedback pieces from surveys, Steam, and X, sorting them into researcher-defined themes. The team found Decision-1 competitive with GPT-6 Sol on quality while running over 14 times faster and 200 times cheaper. The Copilot team measured chat and agentic response quality, finding Decision-1 competitive with GPT-5.6 Luna at 100 times the speed. On-call engineers used it for knowledge retrieval across logs, tickets, calls, and messages during live incidents, where it outperformed LLMs on speed and accuracy. Microsoft Discovery applied it to adaptive replanning in scientific experiments, achieving 46 times more consistent scoring than LLM-based approaches at three times the speed, yielding nearly four times faster replanning overall. Microsoft suggests use cases including agent control, model routing, skill-based decisions, data labeling, AI judging, intent analysis, incident routing, data validation, recommendations, search relevance, content classification, code scanning, safety screening, computer and UI use, robotics, and scientific discovery screening. Developers can access Microsoft-Decision-1 in [Microsoft Foundry](https://ai.azure.com/catalog/models/Microsoft-Decision-1) and [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/microsoft/microsoft-decision-1). To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## 📝 Editorial: Billions in Funding, Hundreds of Papers, One Big Leap? AI’s weekly news cycle increasingly resembles two competitions running in parallel: researchers compete to improve intelligence, while investors compete to price its future. This week, Reflection and Mistral supplied new models, TypeSafe supplied another spectacular financing, and Arena supplied a reminder that someone must measure what all this intelligence does. Together, they suggest a market developing interesting ambitions beyond a better chatbot. Reflection introduced Beam, a mixture-of-experts model with 501 billion parameters, of which 23 billion activate per token. Its technical story centers on reinforcement learning and inference efficiency: Reflection reports generating more than 100 million training rollouts and achieving competitive reasoning performance with substantially less estimated inference compute than some larger rivals. Those estimates are not measured deployment costs, and the weights remain promised for later this month. Still, the proposition matters: agents that execute lengthy workflows need intelligence with an operating budget. Mistral offered a European counterpart with Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk. The trillion-parameter multimodal model entered public API preview, with weights scheduled for release by month’s end. Mistral emphasizes coding, cybersecurity, finance, and law, alongside training on infrastructure it operates in Europe. My reading is that sovereignty is becoming a product feature. For an enterprise, choosing a model also means choosing who controls deployment, customization, and continued access. An impressive benchmark cannot answer those questions. OpenAI added a more fundamental dimension: intelligence contributing to mathematical discovery. The company released more than 700 manuscripts from an unreleased model, reporting progress on open research problems and supplying Lean formalizations for a portion of the results. Verification remains unfinished, and several manuscripts have already been corrected or withdrawn. That distinction matters: generating a plausible proof and establishing mathematical knowledge are different achievements. Yet the possibility is extraordinary. AI could accelerate research enough that checking, interpreting, and connecting its results becomes a central bottleneck. Arena’s question—can we trust what the model did?—suddenly extends from enterprise workflows to the foundations of science. TypeSafe’s $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $7.5 billion valuation, put a price on a different architectural bet. Its Jev model produces typed decisions with confidence estimates that software can consume directly. Consider the thousands of small judgments inside a business process: classify this request, select a tool, escalate this exception. These decisions offer a plausible market for specialized intelligence. The valuation assumes that market will be enormous. You can update your choices at any time in your [settings](https://www.linkedin.com/mypreferences/g/guest-cookies). ![]() # AI Startup Team Execution Criteria Explore top LinkedIn content from expert professionals. ![View profile for Priyanka Vergadia]() #1 Visual Storyteller in Tech and AI | Product Marketing, Developer Relations | TED Speaker | Educator | 300K+ Dev Community | Bestselling Author 2X If you’re leading AI initiatives, here is a strategic cheat sheet to move from "𝗰𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼" to 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲. Think Risk, ROI, and Scalability. This strategy moves you from "𝘄𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹" to "𝘄𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁." 𝟭. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝗪𝗵𝘆" 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲 (𝗣𝗿𝗲-𝗣𝗼𝗖) • Don’t build just because you can. Define the Business Problem first • Success: Is the potential value > 10x the estimated cost? • Decision: If the problem can be solved with Regex or SQL, kill the AI project now. 𝟮. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝗳 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁 (𝗣𝗼𝗖) • Goal: Prove feasibility, not scalability. • Timebox: 4–6 weeks max. • Team: 1-2 AI Engineers + 1 Domain Expert (Data Scientist alone is not enough). • Metric: Technical feasibility (e.g., "Can the model actually predict X with >80% accuracy on historical data?") 𝟯. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝗠𝗩𝗣" 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗗𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵) • Shift from "Notebook" to "System." • Infrastructure: Move off local GPUs to a dev cloud environment. Containerize. • Data Pipeline: Replace manual CSV dumps with automated data ingestion. • Decision: Does the model work on new, unseen data? If accuracy drops >10%, halt and investigate "Data Drift." 𝟰. 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸 & 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝗟𝗮𝘄𝘆𝗲𝗿" 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲) • Compliance is not an afterthought. • Guardrails: Implement checks to prevent hallucination or toxic output (e.g., NeMo Guardrails, Guidance). • Risk Decision: What is the cost of a wrong answer? If high (e.g., medical advice), keep a "Human-in-the-Loop." 𝟱. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 • Scalability & Latency: Users won’t wait 10 seconds for a token. • Serving: Use optimized inference engines (vLLM, TGI, Triton) • Cost Control: Implement token limits and caching. "Pay-as-you-go" can bankrupt you overnight if an API loop goes rogue. 𝟲. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 • Automated Eval: Use "LLM-as-a-Judge" to score outputs against a golden dataset. • Feedback Loops: Build a mechanism for users to Thumbs Up/Down outcomes. Gold for fine-tuning later. 𝟳. Open Source AI.title: Cryptomining malware used poetry to infect more than 3,400 servers, researchers say — four words in the PoeLLM verse, changed 11 times, point the botnet to new servers | Tom's Hardware
Open Source AI.titleZh: Cryptomining malware used poetry to infect more than 3,400 servers, researchers say — four words in the PoeLLM verse, changed 11 times, point the botnet to new servers | Tom's Hardware
Open Source AI.content: # Cryptomining malware used poetry to infect more than 3,400 servers, researchers say — four words in the PoeLLM verse, changed 11 times, point the botnet to new servers Likeliest path into LiteLLM servers was a bug with a fix since April. Over 3,400 “victim servers” were hit by cryptomining malware PoeLLM during a campaign named Canto Incognito, tracked since April 2026, Lumen’s cybersecurity research team Black Lotus Labs reports. The malware’s “command-and-control (C2) mechanism” used address encoding through four words in a two-stanza poem on GitHub, altered 11 times so far, to direct affected hosts to new C2 servers. Most of those hit look to be running “vulnerable versions of open-source AI/LLM services, such as LiteLLM and Ollama,” despite an April LiteLLM fix that probably patched the exploitation path. The malware’s payload consists of XMRig and Iron miners, connected to Kryptex mining infrastructure, with infected servers becoming scanners and exploit servers. The “primary commonality amongst the first 900 victims” was contact with “an endpoint for the Russian crypto mining service,” Lumen says. This indicates that it may be financially motivated. “AI infrastructure is becoming an attractive target” because exposed AI services may contain valuable data and hardware access, especially GPUs. In the meantime, it has “blocked all traffic to and from the PoeLLM C2 servers.” The primary targets are LiteLLM, a proxy server (AI Gateway) to call LLM APIs, a way companies can route their apps to many models through one endpoint, and Gotenberg, a Docker-based API for PDF conversion, which has a guide warning not to expose it to the internet. Also hit are Ollama, which allows you to run open-weight models on your own hardware, although it is not internet-exposed by default, and Gitea, a self-hosted Git platform. Ivanti Sentry, an enterprise gateway appliance, “may also have been targeted,” and one instance was how Lumen discovered the campaign. Although the malware’s methodology involves leveraging poetry, this is only for pointing the infected servers to the C2 server. It is not a form of an AI jailbreak through harmful requests or prompt injection, or what is known as “adversarial poetry,” described in a paper last year. The poem, “On the Nature of Connection,” was first committed in April, with each new version pointing to a new C2 server. The malware is able to decode the new address by pulling specific words and converting them into an IPv4 address. Lumen says that “the malware creator has not changed the pattern used in deciphering the poem” at the time of reporting. Using a poem likely aided in obfuscation as it is “a perfect vehicle for hiding an important message,” the researchers told The Register. The malware is “deployed through vulnerability exploitation of publicly exposed services,” with broad scanning beginning in May. For LiteLLM, a crafted POST to the connection endpoint “was likely the exploitation path,” based on a flaw where two endpoints would run a supplied command on the host with no role check (CVE-2026-42271), which CISA added to its list of exploited vulnerabilities in June. Lumen didn’t detail the methods for Ollama, Gotenberg, and Gitea. If you want to check your own systems, look at connection logs for the indicators of compromise listed on Lumen’s GitHub page. Be sure to audit external exposure when installing any open-source tool and close unnecessary ports. Patch any and all network devices. Follow the individual advisories for the vulnerable products — LiteLLM 1.83.7 or later and Ivanti Sentry R10.5.2, R10.6.2, or R10.7.1. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English #AI # Torvalds says he "really likes using AI" as Linux community debates LLM rules • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •4 min read Share this article Linus Torvalds has waded into the Linux community's debate over AI-generated code and contributions, saying he "really likes using AI" for development work, even as maintainers weigh new rules around LLM-generated content. Linus Torvalds has weighed in on one of the Linux kernel community's most contentious debates: how to handle AI-generated code and contributions. Speaking as the project's longtime leader, Torvalds said he "really likes using AI" for his own development work, a statement that lands in the middle of an ongoing discussion among maintainers about whether and how to regulate LLM-generated patches. The debate isn't hypothetical. Kernel maintainers have been fielding an increasing volume of patches that appear to be generated or heavily assisted by large language models. Some of these contributions are useful; others are low-quality noise that wastes reviewer time. That tension has pushed the community to consider formal rules, including requirements that contributors disclose AI assistance. Torvalds' comments cut through the procedural talk. He didn't position himself as an AI evangelist or a skeptic. He described a practical workflow: he uses AI tools because they help him get work done. That's a notable stance from someone who has built a reputation for blunt, no-nonsense technical judgment. The reaction from the community has been mixed. Some developers see Torvalds' endorsement as a signal that AI-assisted development is here to stay and that the kernel project should adapt. Others worry that his influence could steer the conversation away from the disclosure requirements some maintainers want. ## What the community is actually arguing about The core question isn't whether AI tools are useful. Most developers who have tried modern coding assistants agree they can speed up boilerplate work, suggest reasonable patterns, and help with unfamiliar APIs. The friction comes from accountability and quality control. A human contributor who submits a patch can explain their reasoning, defend their design choices, and iterate on feedback. An AI-generated patch arrives with no such context. Reviewers have to reverse-engineer the intent behind the code, which is harder when the submitter themselves may not fully understand what the model produced. There's also the volume problem. LLMs make it cheap to generate plausible-looking code at scale. A single person can flood a mailing list with dozens of patches that look superficially reasonable but fail under scrutiny. That's a real burden on a volunteer review corps that already has more work than time. Some maintainers have proposed mandatory disclosure: if you used AI to write or substantially assist with a patch, say so. Others argue that disclosure requirements are unenforceable and that the review process should judge the code on its merits regardless of how it was produced. ## Torvalds' practical take Torvalds didn't engage with the policy debate directly in his remarks. He spoke as a developer who has found genuine utility in the tools. His framing suggests he sees AI as another tool in the kit, not a category of contribution that needs special handling. That perspective carries weight. The Linux kernel is one of the largest and most rigorously reviewed software projects in existence. If its leader finds AI assistance genuinely useful for his own work, that's a data point other developers will weigh heavily. It also complicates the case for strict disclosure rules. If the project's most prominent developer is using AI tools as part of his normal workflow, drawing a clean line between "human-written" and "AI-assisted" code becomes even harder. Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/qFaKvbVc5cE/hqdefault.jpg) [Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qFaKvbVc5cE) GuestDhruv Nathawani 4 hours ago00:55:13en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[AI Engineer](/podcast?source=AI%20Engineer) ## Key Takeaways NVIDIA's Dhruv Nathawani demonstrates Data Designer for building synthetic search-agent training data, showing Wikidata-seeded riddles and Tavily trajectories lifted Nemotron Nano's BrowseComp score from 0 to 30 percent. ## Summary The most useful thing in this 55-minute workshop is not the headline topic of "teaching agents to search" — that is the final third of the talk. Most of the session is a working tutorial on NVIDIA's open-source **Data Designer** framework for synthetic data generation, and the search case study is the payoff that demonstrates the method. The central claim, made by NVIDIA research scientist Dhruv Nathawani, is that the hard part of building agent capabilities is not the model but the data pipeline: you take a target agent behavior, turn it into a data problem, generate diverse synthetic data grounded in real-world seeds, filter it aggressively, and only then train. His headline result: using this approach, NVIDIA moved its Nemotron model from 0% to 30% on the BrowseComp search benchmark, and from 26% to 41% on the Bird text-to-SQL benchmark. Nathawani walks through three notebooks — Data Designer basics, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool-calling data, and end-to-end agentic search — and is candid that he "blazed through" the first two because the search notebook is the crux. He also spends the last stretch on a topic he says is genuinely unsolved: how to evaluate synthetic data, illustrated by a concrete failure where his own Wikidata seed had gone stale. The reader should walk away with the framework's abstractions (seed columns, sampler columns, LLM columns, LLM-as-judge), the specific numbers behind the Nemotron search dataset, and a clear-eyed view of the evaluation gap. Dhruv Nathawani is a research scientist at NVIDIA and part of the Nemotron team, which builds NVIDIA's open-source foundation models. He presented this as a one-hour workshop (a prior version ran two hours), with notebooks and slides in a public GitHub repo referenced by a recurring QR code. ## Data Designer turns a target agent behavior into a data pipeline The framework's core premise is that internet data is not the data you want for a transformer — a quote Nathawani attributes to Andrej Karpathy — because internet data ranges from high-quality sources like Wikipedia to random opinions on X. The traditional approach is to curate that data; Data Designer's approach is to generate synthetic data either from scratch or from a seed dataset, so the output is "grounded in real-world distribution and real-world data" rather than purely model-invented. Nathawani is explicit about why naive generation fails. If you just loop an LLM a million times asking for a product, a review, and a customer profile, you get repetition after 10–20 iterations, no correlations between features, no multimodality, no steering, no validation, and no way to share the process with a colleague. Data Designer's answer is to generate data **column by column** and assemble the columns into a DAG that describes the dataset; when the DAG is ready, one execution produces the dataset. | Column type | Purpose | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Seed column | Optional grounding data | Wikipedia topics, company CSV/JSON/Parquet | | Sampler column | Inject diversity via Python | Question difficulty: easy / medium / hard, with weights | | Sub-sampler | Map a sampler value to a subtype | "Easy" → direct lookup; "Hard" → obscure detail | | LLM text column | Generate free text | Trivi...

[Submit an Article](https://write.insightmediagroup.io) [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/towards-data-science/)[X](https://x.com/TDataScience) [LLM Applications](/category/artificial-intelligence/llm-applications/) # A Practical Guide to OpenAI's New Decisions API Is this the JEV killer? [Thomas Reid](/author/thomas_reid/) October 11, 202611 min read ![](https://assets.insightmediagroup.io/media/1791463767654_gchmb3.webp) Image by AI I recently covered TypesafeAI’s JEVin TDS (link at the end). JEV makes fast decisions, such as classifying content or choosing the next step in a workflow, and returns typed answers that software can use directly. The accompanying probabilities help an application decide whether to act on an answer or pass it to a person for review. The internet went a bit crazy over JEV, so it was no surprise to see rival products appear after its release. Among the most prominent was the Decisions API that OpenAI previewed at its recent DevDay and made available as a public beta shortly after. In this article, I’ll look at the new API, how to get it, and some practical use-case examples, and I’ll let you know whether I think it’s a JEV killer or whether TypesafeAI can sleep soundly at night. ## The background to JEV-like models Suppose you run an online shop. A customer writes to say that their keyboard arrived with three broken keys and asks for a replacement. Before anyone replies, your application needs to decide which team should handle the message. You could ask a language model to classify it and return JSON. But the application only needs a category and enough information to decide whether to trust that category. That process could also be relatively slow and costly if it had to handle 1000s of requests. OpenAI’s Decisions API gives that operation its own endpoint. Additionally, OpenAI claims its Decisions API can make decisions up to ten times faster than GPT-6 Luna, the LLM that Decisions is based on, through the Responses API. To explore how it works, we’ll walk through three Python examples and compare OpenAI’s approach with TypesafeAI’s JEV model. One major advantage of the Decisions API over JEV is that it can handle images. Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Amazon Nears $7 Billion Deal for AI Startup Decart, WSJ Says [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Amazon is in talks to acquire AI startup Decart in a deal valued at approximately $7 billion, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter. Decart, founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, develops software that lets developers switch AI workloads between chips from different vendors and builds world models such as Lucy and Oasis for simulating real-world environments. Amazon previously gave Decart early access to its Trainium3 chip in 2025. The startup was valued at nearly $4 billion in May and had drawn acquisition interest from Anthropic at around $6 billion in September. ##### Key Elements ![Amazon Nears $7 Billion Deal for AI Startup Decart, WSJ Says](https://img.biggo.com/u34-ZHWMLrYTHPnQvEJFh-i0ZSrAhcLhs5A3foGS4Cw/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzcwY2Q3Y2Y2LTYwMTctNGQxYy1iNzY4LWQ5MjU0MDg2MjlhZl8xNzkxNzY1NDcxX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) is in advanced discussions to acquire Decart, an Israeli artificial intelligence startup that develops software for optimizing AI workloads across different chip architectures, in a transaction that could value the company at roughly $7 billion, according to a Wall Street Journal report on Sunday. The talks could produce an agreement in short order if negotiations do not break down, people familiar with the matter told the newspaper. A successful deal would deepen Amazon's vertical integration in AI, stitching together its in-house silicon, cloud infrastructure and application layer. Decart, founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, has built a software platform that lets developers move AI training and inference workloads between chips from different vendors with minimal friction. That capability has grown more valuable as enterprises look to reduce their dependence on any single GPU supplier, particularly as demand for compute continues to outstrip supply. The startup has also pushed into what it calls world models, a category of AI systems designed to simulate and interact with real-world environments. Its Lucy model processes and edits video in real time, while Oasis generates interactive simulations that can be used to train and test physical AI systems such as autonomous vehicles and robots. Amazon's interest in Decart is not new. The cloud computing giant gave the startup early access to Trainium3, its third-generation custom AI chip, in 2025. Acquiring Decart would give Amazon a software layer purpose-built to bridge its proprietary silicon with customer workloads, a move that could strengthen AWS's position against Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) in the AI infrastructure market. Decart was valued at nearly $4 billion in May, meaning the reported $7 billion price tag would represent a substantial premium in under six months. The startup had previously drawn acquisition interest from Anthropic, which considered a deal at around $6 billion in September before walking away after conducting due diligence. The deal talks come as Amazon accelerates its push into AI infrastructure. The company has positioned Trainium as a lower-cost alternative to Nvidia's dominant GPU lineup, and AWS has been aggressively courting AI developers with credits, managed services and custom silicon. Bringing Decart in-house would give Amazon a talent base and technology stack that directly addresses one of the thorniest problems in enterprise AI: portability across heterogeneous hardware. For developers, the appeal of Decart's software lies in its ability to abstract away chip-level differences. Infra & Chips.content: [Home](/en) Article # The AI sector is most short of exit buyers. 36氪的朋友们2026-10-11 13:47 The Unavoidable Bottlenecks and Opportunities in AI Computing Power Recently, ByteDance secured a USD 29.6 billion syndicated loan, Alibaba completed a HKD 80 billion share placement, and a few months prior, Google and Amazon raised over USD 800 billion in total financing, while NVIDIA announced a "grand plan" worth USD 500 billion. All major tech corporations around the world are scrambling to raise capital, and they are investing the funds in one single direction: AI infrastructure. From a macro perspective, every underlying opportunity that reshapes the industrial landscape in modern industrial history is essentially a top-tier infrastructure upgrade. The vigorous railway mania and the Gold Rush in the western United States in the 19th century, the real estate urbanization drive in China, and the current global AI infrastructure boom — although the process of massive capital injection is likely to be constantly marred by market disputes and accompanied by bubbles, the infrastructure finally precipitated will firmly underpin industrial development for decades to come. However, compared with previous global infrastructure waves, this round of AI infrastructure has a wider coverage, an unprecedented scale of capital investment, far faster industrial iteration, and naturally more disputes. In July, AI infrastructure experienced a sharp fluctuation, as the capital market began to question the gap between the huge investment in AI infrastructure and the returns it could generate. The extensive era of mindlessly stacking GPUs and frantically expanding clusters has not ended yet, but the market is starting to wonder: after trillions of dollars are invested in computing power, can we really make profits in the future? This marks a signal of changes in both the capital side and the industrial side. The difference from last year is that this year, people can clearly feel that ordinary users have begun to use various desktop Agents on a regular basis. AI is no longer a simple chat tool, but has truly become an agent that can run automatically and perform tasks in cycles. This year is the real first year of Agent. The widespread popularization of C-end agents has also made Token consumption continuously exceed expectations. In March this year, the average daily Token call volume in China exceeded 140 trillion, which was more than 1,000 times higher than that at the beginning of 2024. However, there is a rather awkward problem at present. Everyone is shouting that there is a shortage of GPUs and competing for computing power, but in fact, a large number of GPUs are idling, lying unused and wasted every day. Carnegie Mellon University conducted an actual test, running 756 GPUs continuously for 31 days, and found that nearly 20% of the cluster's time was spent in "waiting". For example, for OpenAI's inference business, more than half of the energy consumption is wasted on idling; the situation of domestic intelligent computing centers is even more extreme, with the average GPU utilization rate less than 30%. In the past few years, AI infrastructure grew wildly, and the expansion of scale could cover up the efficiency problem. But now that the time for returns is approaching, the competition lies in who can reduce the Token cost and increase the computing power utilization rate. Efficiency has become the new key to success for AI Infra. Therefore, the urgent issues now are how to revitalize the idling computing power and how to reduce the inference cost. As the AI Infra market enters the deep water zone, industry noise is gradually increasing. The AI track is expanding too broadly, with chips, power, hardware, software, models, and applications stacked layer upon layer. The plan is to combine the two companies' technology and customer networks to target corporations that require large-scale AI compute resources. Naver Cloud said on the 12th that it recently signed a business agreement at its headquarters, "1784," with FPT to cooperate on the AI Factory and GPU as a Service (GPUaaS) businesses. The companies will discuss cooperation plans from planning to development and operations for the AI Factory business. FPT, an Nvidia Cloud Partner, is running an AI cloud business in Vietnam. The two companies will link their respective GPU infrastructure and cloud technology and jointly identify demand in regions that are difficult to address individually. By providing GPU resources for AI training and inference, as well as AI models and services, they will help customers reduce the expense and burden of building their own infrastructure. They will also promote exchanges among technical personnel. Engineers from Naver Cloud headquarters, the Vietnam development center, and FPT will regularly share technology and jointly carry out on-site tasks for customers, such as optimizing GPU infrastructure, improving inference performance, and building environments for AI agent services. ※ This article has been translated by AI.
